claims.text: In noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles under rapid heating and cooling, retention of a metastable single-phase solid solution is governed by high-temperature residence time and element-specific atomic mobility.
Very rapid cooling kinetically traps a chemically homogeneous state despite potentially unfavorable thermodynamics.
Deliberately slower cooling through a temperature window of appreciable atomic mobility permits elemental segregation.
Au and Cu preferentially segregate to nanoparticle surfaces.
Au and Cu surface segregation is caused by their lower surface energies.
Surface segregation of Au and Cu promotes phase separation.
Cooling-induced segregation nucleates secondary phases and transforms the material away from the intended single-phase structure.
During rapid heating, all constituent elements decompose and become atomically mobile.
An extremely brief high-temperature exposure prevents significant diffusion and thereby preserves a homogeneous single-phase structure.
Slower cooling provides sufficient time for atoms to overcome kinetic barriers and diffuse to surfaces and interfaces.
Relative to rapid quenching, slower cooling will produce detectable enrichment of Au and Cu at particle surfaces.
Relative to rapid quenching, slower cooling will produce secondary phases and altered diffraction patterns.
The proposed mechanism applies to near-equimolar nanoparticles containing more than five noble and other metal elements.
The proposed mechanism applies under rapid-heating, high-peak-temperature processing where diffusion becomes significant during cooling.
Outside the stated composition and processing regime, equilibrium or other kinetic pathways may dominate.
Rapid heating followed by immediate quenching can yield a metastable, single-phase solid-solution baseline.
A lack of statistically significant segregation or phase-separation differences between slower-cooled and rapidly quenched samples would falsify the proposed cooling-controlled mechanism.
